name: Buenos Aires
tagline: A European-grand capital of tango, beef and late nights.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, May, Jun, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Autumn in March-April and spring in October-November are finest, with jacaranda purple in November. Avoid the humid January heat.

ourTake.lede: Buenos Aires keeps late hours, and fighting that rhythm is the surest way to miss it. Eat at ten, take the milonga after midnight, and reserve mornings for slow walks through Recoleta and Palermo rather than early starts. Skip the staged dinner-tango shows aimed at tour groups; a neighbourhood milonga, even just to watch, is the real thing.
ourTake.comeIf: You want tango, exceptional steak and Malbec, and a European-feeling city at the far edge of the map.
ourTake.skipIf: You keep strictly vegetarian or want a short flight; this is a long haul into a meat-and-wine city.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Buenos Aires
items.description: A modern tower and a restored 1916 Belle Époque mansion (La Mansión) side by side in Recoleta, the city's most complete grand hotel, and its most decorated.

items.name: Palacio Duhau, Park Hyatt Buenos Aires
items.description: A 1930s French-style palace joined to a modern wing by an art-lined garden tunnel, terraced gardens, a cheese room and quietly impeccable Recoleta grandeur.

items.name: Alvear Palace Hotel
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The 1932 gilded grande dame of Avenida Alvear, Louis XV and XVI furnishings, white-gloved butlers and a century of Argentine high-society ceremony.

items.name: Palacio Duhau, Park Hyatt (Palacio-wing suites)
items.description: The palace-wing suites of the Duhau, grand proportions, French mouldings and garden or Avenida Alvear views, with the full Park Hyatt service.

items.name: Four Seasons Buenos Aires, La Mansión suites
items.description: The seven suites within the restored 1916 mansion, the most exclusive rooms in the city, with private grandeur and the full Four Seasons hand.

items.name: Faena Hotel Buenos Aires
items.description: Philippe Starck's theatrical red-and-white fantasy inside a converted 1902 grain mill, unicorn statues, a cabaret hall and pure Argentine drama on the docks.

items.name: Casa Lucía
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A 1929 Bencich-family building on Avenida Santa Fe reborn as a warm, art-filled modern house, timber, brass and a rooftop pool over the city.

items.name: Alvear Icon Hotel
credentials: Alvear maison (sister to The Leading Hotels of the World Alvear Palace)
items.description: The Alvear group's sleek modern tower on the Puerto Madero waterfront, high floors, river and city views and a rooftop pool and spa.

items.name: Hotel Madero
items.description: A polished contemporary hotel on the Puerto Madero docks, a rooftop pool, a spa and a quiet, well-run calm a short walk from the old town.

items.name: La Recoleta Cemetery
items.description: A hushed marble city of the dead where 4,691 above-ground vaults, Evita Perón's among them, line avenues of angels and domes. A private guide turns the sprawl into an hour of storytelling that even restless teenagers fall quiet for; go early, before the coach groups arrive.

items.name: Teatro Colón
credentials: Rated among the world's top three opera houses for acoustics by National Geographic
items.description: Argentina's grand opera house, ranked among the world's finest for acoustics, Pavarotti said its perfection made him nervous. A box for the evening, or a private daytime tour of the golden horseshoe auditorium and marble Salón Dorado, is the city at its most refined.

items.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes
items.description: The finest art collection in Latin America, Goya, Rembrandt, Rodin, Monet, Van Gogh and the deepest holding of Argentine masters, all with free entry. A civilised, air-conditioned hour between lunch and the cemetery, easily paced for grandparents.

items.name: Plaza de Mayo
items.description: The historic heart of the nation, framed by the pink Casa Rosada, the colonial Cabildo and the Cathedral, the square where Evita addressed the masses and the Mothers still march on Thursdays. A guide unpacks two centuries of Argentine drama in one walkable block.

items.name: Casa Rosada
items.description: The rose-pink presidential palace whose famous balcony framed Evita, and, for many, the ghost of the Broadway song. Free weekend tours reveal the halls of power, or simply admire the facade from the plaza on a private history walk.

items.name: Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral
items.description: Behind a Greek-temple facade lies the country's principal church, where Jorge Bergoglio said mass before becoming Pope Francis, and where General San Martín's remains rest under permanent guard. Quietly moving even for non-Catholic visitors.

items.name: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
credentials: Named the world's most beautiful bookstore by National Geographic (2019)
items.description: A 1919 theatre, frescoed ceiling, crimson stage curtain, opera boxes intact, reborn as a bookshop where you browse novels from the old balcony seats. A magical, unhurried stop the whole family enjoys, coffee served on the former stage.

items.name: Avenida 9 de Julio & the Obelisco
items.description: The city's Champs-Élysées and Eiffel Tower in one, reputedly the world's widest avenue, crowned by the 67-metre Obelisco. Best seen at dusk from a private car as the traffic-light rivers begin to glow.

items.name: Don Julio
items.description: The parrilla that turned the Argentine steak into world-class theatre, Angus and Hereford dry-aged in its own butchery, poured with a wall of Malbec. Book weeks ahead and let the maître d' arrange a private table; the kitchen handles vegetarians and grilled-vegetable feasts with real care when told in advance.

items.name: San Telmo Sunday Market
items.description: Every Sunday, Defensa Street becomes ten blocks of antiques, silver, leather and buskers, converging on cobbled Plaza Dorrego where couples still dance tango as the light fades. A guide keeps the crowd manageable and steers you to the genuine dealers, not the trinket stalls.

items.name: Caminito & La Boca
items.description: The postcard lane of tin houses painted in leftover shipyard colours, where tango was born among Genoese dockworkers. Best enjoyed mid-morning with a private guide who keeps you within the safe tourist blocks and adds the real immigrant history behind the pretty facades.

items.name: Puente de la Mujer & Puerto Madero
items.description: Calatrava's white 'Woman's Bridge', a stylised tango dancer in steel, arcs over the old docks, now the city's polished riverside quarter of glass towers and terraced restaurants. An easy, flat evening stroll before a waterside dinner, safe and pram-friendly.

items.name: MALBA (Museo de Arte Latinoamericano)
items.description: Costantini's private collection turned public: Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, Tarsila do Amaral and the giants of Latin American modernism in a cool, light-filled building. Compact enough for an afternoon, with an excellent café for a pause.

items.name: Bosques de Palermo (Parque Tres de Febrero)
items.description: The city's green lungs, 400 hectares of lakes, jacaranda and rowing boats, laid out by landscape master Carlos Thays. A gentle morning for multi-generational groups: pedal boats for the children, shaded benches for the elders.

items.name: El Rosedal (Palermo Rose Garden)
credentials: Protected as part of Buenos Aires' Cultural Heritage
items.description: More than 8,000 roses across 90-odd species, pergolas and a poets' garden inside the Bosques, the park's most beloved corner and a florid backdrop for family photographs. Free, serene, and at its peak in the southern spring (October–November).

items.name: Jardín Japonés
items.description: One of the largest Japanese gardens outside Japan, gifted for a royal visit, koi ponds, red bridges, a teahouse and clipped calm minutes from the city rush. A restful, veg-friendly lunch stop that particularly delights grandparents.

items.name: Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Pilar
items.description: The whitewashed colonial jewel beside the cemetery, its original 18th-century Peruvian silver altars still intact, with a small cloister museum upstairs. A five-minute, deeply atmospheric pairing with a Recoleta cemetery visit.

items.name: Floralis Genérica
items.description: A 20-metre steel-and-aluminium flower that opens its petals at dawn and closes them at dusk, mirrored in a reflecting pool, the city's modern icon. A free, photogenic pause on the way between the Fine Arts museum and the law faculty.

items.name: Centro Cultural Recoleta
items.description: A former convent turned contemporary-arts complex, rotating exhibitions, design shows and a rooftop that catches the afternoon light, right beside the cemetery and basilica. A cool, unhurried counterpoint to the neighbourhood's grand history.

items.name: Rojo Tango at Faena
items.description: Tango's most exclusive show: a red-velvet cabaret for barely a hundred guests inside Philippe Starck's Faena Hotel, so close you feel the bandoneón. The discreet, luxurious choice for couples and small parties who want spectacle without a tourist crowd.

items.name: Café de los Angelitos tango show
items.description: A grand dinner-and-show in an 1890 café once frequented by Carlos Gardel himself, the most complete traditional tango experience, with a full orchestra and a Malbec-paired menu. Vegetarian courses available on request; ideal for a first, immersive night of tango.

items.name: Café Tortoni
credentials: Designated a Notable Bar of Buenos Aires
items.description: The city's oldest café, founded in 1858, where Borges and Gardel once sat beneath stained glass and marble columns. A living relic, order a submarino (hot milk with a bar of chocolate) and soak up a slower Buenos Aires.

items.name: Argentine Open Polo Championship (Palermo)
items.description: The world's most prestigious polo tournament, played each November–December at the 'Cathedral of Polo' since 1928, where 40-goal teams draw crowds of 30,000. Box seats, an asado and a chilled Malbec make it the season's grand social occasion for Indian polo enthusiasts.

items.name: Estancia day trip, San Antonio de Areco
items.description: Ninety minutes onto the pampas to a working estancia, gaucho horsemanship, folk music, an open-fire asado and optional polo lessons in the birthplace of Argentine gaucho tradition. A private full-day escape that lands beautifully with families and riders.

items.name: Colonia del Sacramento day trip (Uruguay)
items.description: A one-hour fast ferry across the Río de la Plata to Uruguay's oldest town, cobbled Portuguese-Spanish lanes, a lighthouse and riverside cafés, walkable in an afternoon. Passports and a private transfer make for an effortless second-country stamp.

items.name: Tigre Delta
items.description: An hour north, the Paraná fans into a maze of green islands, stilt houses and rowing clubs best explored by private launch, with the Puerto de Frutos market to browse afterwards. A cooling, scenic day on the water for all ages.

items.name: El Zanjón de Granados
items.description: Beneath an 1830 mansion lies a restored labyrinth of brick tunnels and cisterns tracing 400 years of the city's foundations, a private, atmospheric hour few tourists know. The most rewarding hidden gem in San Telmo.

items.name: Museo Nacional de Arte Decorativo (Palacio Errázuriz)
items.description: A French Beaux-Arts palace by the architect of Buenos Aires' grandest mansions, its rooms hung with El Greco, Manet and Rodin, the only such house that opens regularly to the public. A jewel-box afternoon for lovers of design and la belle époque.

items.name: Palacio Paz (Círculo Militar)
items.description: The largest private house ever built in Argentina, 140 rooms of Louvre-inspired grandeur, a soaring domed rotunda and marble halls, now open by guided tour. Occasional evening tours pair the palace with a lyrical concert or wine tasting.

items.name: Fundación Proa
items.description: La Boca's serious side: a sleek glass-and-steel contemporary art centre with world-class temporary shows and a rooftop café overlooking the Riachuelo. A refined, safe anchor before or after the colourful chaos of Caminito.

items.name: Palermo Soho
items.description: The city's most stylish quarter, independent designers, leather ateliers, art galleries and pavement cafés radiating from leafy Plaza Serrano. The place to shop for one-off pieces and graze between boutiques; a personal shopper smooths the way.

items.name: Palermo Hollywood
items.description: Palermo's cooler, more grown-up cousin, threaded with acclaimed restaurants, cocktail bars and cinema-studio history, coming alive after 10pm as Argentines do. Ideal for a long, late dinner and a nightcap without the backpacker throng.

items.name: Vinoteca at Palacio Duhau – Park Hyatt
items.description: A cellar of 500-plus labels inside a restored palace, where a sommelier walks you through blind Malbec flights paired with the kitchen's small plates. A discreet, luxurious way to learn Argentine wine without leaving the city.

items.name: Puerta cerrada (closed-door) dinner
items.description: Argentina's intimate answer to fine dining, a home turned private restaurant seating a handful of guests, with sommelier hosts and a multi-course, wine-paired menu. Bookable exclusively for your party, and happy to build a vegetarian tasting when asked.

items.name: Avenida de Mayo & Palacio Barolo
items.description: The stately Parisian boulevard linking the Casa Rosada to Congress, crowned by the Palacio Barolo, a 1923 tower designed as a stone homage to Dante's Divine Comedy, with a lighthouse-topped viewpoint. A guided climb rewards you with one of the city's best panoramas.

items.name: Congreso de la Nación
items.description: The green-domed national Congress closing Avenida de Mayo, a Greco-Roman monument to Argentine democracy with free guided tours of its chambers and library. A grand architectural bookend to a historic-centre walk.

items.name: Galerías Pacífico
items.description: A belle-époque shopping arcade under a frescoed cupola painted by Argentina's leading muralists, luxury boutiques below fine art above, on pedestrian Calle Florida. Elegant browsing and a cultural centre make it a rainy-afternoon refuge.

items.name: Milonga at Salón Canning / La Catedral
items.description: Not a show but the real thing, a social dance hall where porteños of every age dance tango until dawn, from grand parquet salons to bohemian converted warehouses. A guide or private teacher lets you watch (or step in) with the etiquette right.

items.name: Feria de Mataderos
items.description: A weekend fair on the city's edge where gauchos ride, folk musicians play and the pampas comes to town, crafts, empanadas and a horseback skill game called the sortija. The most authentic, least touristy folk experience in Buenos Aires, best reached by private car.

items.name: Museo Evita
items.description: Set in a 1920s mansion Evita once ran as a shelter, this intimate museum traces her extraordinary rise through gowns, film and photographs. Essential context for anyone moved by her story at Recoleta, and easily paired with a Palermo lunch.

items.name: Planetario Galileo Galilei
items.description: A striking modernist sphere on three arches inside the Bosques, with immersive dome shows and lakeside lawns around it. A fun, air-conditioned hour for families with children, and a photogenic landmark at dusk.

items.name: Chacarita's La Chacra & the parrilla circuit
items.description: Beyond Don Julio, a private steak-and-wine crawl through the city's best asadores, La Cabrera, Parrilla Peña, Niño Gordo, is a delicious education in cuts, chimichurri and provoleta. A knowledgeable guide secures the tables and translates the grill.

items.name: Aramburu
items.description: Gonzalo Aramburu's precise, artful tasting menu, the highest gastronomic reference in the country, and Argentina's only two-Michelin-star table.

items.name: Don Julio
items.description: Pablo Rivero's parrilla, the definitive Argentine steakhouse, No. 1 in all of Latin America and a one-star table where the grill is treated as an art.

items.name: Trescha
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024, No. 33 (Highest New Entry)
items.description: Tomás Treschanski's 14-course counter for just ten diners, a young, virtuosic kitchen and the city's most exciting fine-dining seat.

items.name: Chila
items.description: A long-standing fine-dining room on the Puerto Madero docks, a tasting-menu celebration of Argentina's regions and its wines.

items.name: Crizia
items.description: Gabriel Oggero's oyster bar and seafood-driven kitchen in a leafy Palermo townhouse, the newest of the city's Michelin stars.

items.name: El Preferido de Palermo
items.description: A restored 1952 corner bodegón reborn under the Don Julio family, Spanish-Argentine classics, house-cured hams and a joyful, buzzing room.

items.name: Mishiguene
items.description: Tomás Kalika's reimagining of Jewish diaspora cooking, pastrami, babka and shakshuka elevated to a celebrated, soulful fine-dining table.

items.name: Niño Gordo
items.description: A neon-lit, theatrical 'Asian parrilla', Argentine fire cooking crossed with Southeast and East Asian flavours, loud and hugely fun.

items.name: Julia
items.description: A tiny, produce-obsessed neighbourhood kitchen, a short, changing menu of quietly brilliant contemporary cooking from chef Julio Martín Báez.

items.name: Anchoíta
items.description: A farm-to-table kitchen with its own organic plot, Guaraní-inspired sharing plates, house charcuterie, river fish and superb pasta.

items.name: Sacro
items.description: Buenos Aires' most ambitious plant-based kitchen, gourmet vegan cooking, a serious cocktail list and a sleek, grown-up room.

items.name: Elena
credentials: Within Four Seasons Hotel Buenos Aires
items.description: The Four Seasons' dry-aging steakhouse and all-day room, polished Argentine grilling and one of the best Sunday brunches in the city.

items.name: Gran Dabbang
items.description: Mariano Ramón's tiny, riotous storefront where Indian and Southeast Asian spice meets Argentine produce, one of the most loved kitchens in the city.

items.name: Anafe
items.description: A small, chef-led corner bistro celebrated for inventive, produce-driven cooking at an accessible price.

items.name: Café Tortoni
credentials: Historic landmark (est. 1858); a founding member of the world's historic cafés
items.description: The city's most storied café since 1858, stained glass, marble and mirrors, and the ghosts of Borges and Gardel over coffee and churros.

items.name: El Cuartito
credentials: Historic landmark (est. 1934); a Buenos Aires institution
items.description: A beloved 1934 pizzeria plastered in football and boxing memorabilia, thick porteño pizza and fugazzeta the way the city has always eaten it.

items.name: Florería Atlántico
credentials: Rémy Martin Legend Award (pioneer of the scene)
items.description: A flower shop and wine cellar hiding a legendary basement bar, the pioneer of the modern Buenos Aires scene, and a former World's No. 1.

items.name: L'Orangerie (Alvear Palace)
credentials: Within Alvear Palace Hotel, The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The Alvear Palace's glass-roofed salon, crystal chandeliers, monogrammed china and the most ceremonial afternoon tea or aperitif in the city.

items.name: Tres Monos
items.description: A high-energy, no-menu cocktail den with a social conscience, the highest-ranked bar in South America and a genuine world-beater.

items.name: CoChinChina
items.description: Inés de los Santos's theatrical bar where Vietnam and France meet an Argentine accent, polished, glamorous and one of the world's best.

items.name: Presidente Bar
items.description: The grand end of Buenos Aires cocktail culture, chandeliers over a long bar, a winter garden and a library-styled private room.

items.name: Piano Nobile / Oak Bar (Palacio Duhau)
credentials: Within Palacio Duhau, Park Hyatt (MICHELIN Key, 2025)
items.description: The Park Hyatt palace's clubby wood-panelled bar and garden terrace, impeccable classics, a whisky and cognac library and quiet Recoleta calm.

items.name: Trade Sky Bar
items.description: A Gatsby-styled rooftop with 360-degree views over the Obelisk, Puerto Madero and downtown, the city's most glamorous high-up drink.

items.name: Nicky Harrison
credentials: Widely cited Buenos Aires speakeasy (goop; press)
items.description: A Prohibition-era speakeasy hidden behind a sushi counter, password entry, live jazz and a 1920s-with-an-Argentine-twist theatre.

plan.heading: 4 days in Buenos Aires, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into Palacio Duhau – Park Hyatt, then walk the Recoleta Cemetery and the French-quarter mansions around Avenida Alvear.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: See the Malba's Latin American collection, then take an unhurried coffee at the Palacio Duhau's garden terrace.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Elena inside the Four Seasons, the city's finest dry-aged beef and a serious cellar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Wander the leafy streets of Palermo Chico and the botanical garden before the heat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A private tasting of Argentine Malbec and Cabernet Franc, then browse the ateliers of Palermo Soho.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Don Julio, the Palermo parrilla on the World's 50 Best list; book well ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Explore San Telmo's cobbles and antique arcades, quiet before the Sunday crowds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross to the Costanera and Puerto Madero for the river light and the Fortabat art collection.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A tasting menu at Aramburu, the city's refined modern Argentine kitchen, followed by a late private tango.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive out to a working estancia on the pampas for horses and open country.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A slow asado lunch under the trees, then unhurried return to the city.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A quiet final dinner at Chila in Puerto Madero, overlooking the docks.

items.name: Recoleta
items.description: Belle Époque grandeur, the famous cemetery and old money; suits a classic, elegant first stay.

items.name: Palermo (Soho & Chico)
items.description: Leafy, design-led and dense with restaurants and bars; for travellers who want the city's best eating on their doorstep.

items.name: San Telmo
items.description: Cobblestones, antique markets and tango history; atmospheric and bohemian, best for those who like their charm a little rough-edged.

events.name: Tango BA Festival y Mundial
events.note: The world's largest tango gathering, culminating in the World Championship finals at the Gran Rex; free events fill the city.

events.name: Carnaval Porteño
events.note: Neighbourhood murga troupes and free street corsos across more than twenty barrios; a local, unglossed carnival.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Dinner starts late, from 21:00 onward, so plan accordingly; base yourself in Recoleta for grace or Palermo for energy, and a good concierge can secure a table at the hard-to-book parrillas and a private tango salon rather than a tourist show.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Ministro Pistarini (Ezeiza, EZE) for long-haul; a private chauffeur meets you airside and it is a 45-minute run into Recoleta or Palermo, while domestic and regional flights use the closer-in Aeroparque Jorge Newbery (AEP).

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Keep a private car and driver on call for the sprawl, but walk the leafy grids of Recoleta, Palermo and San Telmo, which reward it.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Buy an eSIM (Claro, Movistar or Personal) before landing; 4G is strong across the city and hotel wifi is reliable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Currency is the Argentine peso; carry some US dollars cash for the favourable informal rate, but cards work in better restaurants and hotels; tip around 10 percent.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Southern-hemisphere seasons are flipped: Oct-Nov (spring) and Mar-Apr (autumn) are mild and dry; Dec-Feb is hot and humid with much of the city on holiday, and Jun-Jul can be grey and damp.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; the cleanest one-stop is Doha with Qatar Airways (DOH-EZE nonstop, ~18h in the air plus the India-Doha leg, roughly 24h door to door). Ethiopian via Addis Ababa is the alternative. Fly Qatar Qsuite in business; use the Al Mourjan lounge at Doha and keep a 3-4h buffer on the outbound to absorb the long southern leg.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations for India-origin travellers; routine cover plus Hepatitis A is sensible. Tap water is safe in the city. Buenos Aires is generally safe in Recoleta, Palermo and Puerto Madero; use registered cars, avoid displaying valuables, and be alert to distraction thefts.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Argentina is meat-heavy, but Palermo has strong vegetarian and vegan kitchens; pure-veg is workable, strict Jain (no onion/garlic/root) needs briefing ahead. Indian food is limited but present. Sacro (fine-dining vegan) and the Palermo vegetarian scene are reliable.
